One night, by the harbor fire, Eleazar, an old scribe, tells you a story from about thirty years ago: a child born in Bethlehem, shepherds who ran to see him and some wise men who followed a star. Since then a question has followed you: who is this man?
Micah had written it centuries before: the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem. I’ve read that scroll a hundred times.
In Jerusalem, a nervous king asks about a newborn child. And in Capernaum, your dad’s fever won’t go down.
I saw him once in the temple, at twelve, asking the teachers questions. I never forgot his answers.
Now you live it with your own eyes. You travel with Asher and Eleazar to the Jordan River, where John is baptizing a crowd.
They say the man from the Jordan fasted forty days in the desert and is now coming back to Galilee. To your town.

He talks about seeds, sheep and a father who runs to hug his son. Tonight I realized those stories are about me.
He came in on a donkey and people spread cloaks on the road. Lucius says they want to arrest him. Tomorrow is the Passover and my heart is heavy.
I have no words. The sky went dark and we all fell silent. Eleazar read the scroll of Isaiah and I understood it was all for us. For me.
He’s alive! The women were running, the stone was rolled away and the field woke up full of flowers. The question that followed me all the way finally has an answer.
Bethlehem means house of bread. The one who would later say he is the bread of life was born here, in the house of bread.
From Nazareth to Bethlehem is about 150 kilometers. It was several days on foot along dirt and stone roads, with Mary at the end of her pregnancy.
In Nazareth, every morning you could hear the mill grinding the grain for the day’s bread. Jesus grew up in that simple life.
Two turtledoves or two young pigeons: the offering of families who couldn’t afford a lamb. The owner of everything came to the temple with the offering of the poor.
It holds the Shema, the prayer said every morning and every night. Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is the one Lord, and love him with all your heart.
By this river, John introduced Jesus with a phrase that sums up the gospel: “Look! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!”
Forty years of Israel in the desert, forty days of Moses on the mountain and of Elijah on the road. Where Israel fell in the test, Jesus stayed faithful.
Weak and hungry, Jesus heard the temptation to turn them into bread. He answered with Scripture: people live by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
In 1986 a first-century wooden boat, about 8 meters long, appeared in the mud of this shore. Peter and his companions used a boat like this.
Peter had fished all night without catching anything. Even so he let down the nets where Jesus told him, and both boats nearly sank.
They were for ceremonial washing, about a hundred liters each. At the wedding in Cana, Jesus filled them with new wine in abundance.
Roofs were flat, made of branches and mud. Four friends opened one to lower their paralyzed friend in front of Jesus.
Five barley loaves and two fish, poor people’s food, were enough for thousands. With what was left over they filled twelve baskets.
Zacchaeus couldn’t see because of the crowd, so he ran and climbed a tree like this one. Jesus stopped right there and called him by name.
Unleavened bread because of the hurry to leave, and bitter herbs for the slavery. At this supper, Jesus gave the bread and the cup a new meaning.
When Jesus died, the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom. The way into God’s presence was opened.
At dawn, on the beach, Jesus waited for his friends with fish and bread on the coals. By a fire like this, Peter had denied him.
That night we were watching the sheep here when the glory of the Lord surrounded us. We went running and found the baby just as we had been told.
We brought him three gifts. Gold is for a king, incense is burned for God, and myrrh is used to prepare the dead.
Repent and turn back to God, because the kingdom of heaven is near. After me comes someone far more powerful than I am.
A Samaritan brought me a wounded man on his own donkey. He left me two silver coins to take care of him.
It shows that Jesus is a gift that comes from above, and that being born of a woman he is truly one of us.
Later the leaders were amazed to see ordinary people without schooling, and they realized they had been with Jesus.
Jesus grew in wisdom, in stature, in favor with God and with people. In which one would you like to ask him for help this week?
In the story of the prodigal son, do you feel more like the one who left or the one who stayed angry? The Father runs toward both.
God promises that a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent’s head. It’s the first promise of a Savior.
Through Abraham’s descendants all nations would be blessed. The foreign wise men who come to Bethlehem are the first foretaste.
God promises David a son with a throne that will never end. Jesus is born in Bethlehem, the city of David.
A child called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father and Prince of Peace. In Bethlehem, that promise sleeps in a manger.
The boy Samuel grew in stature and in favor with the Lord and with people. Luke uses almost the same words for Jesus.
Out of Egypt I called my son, God says through Hosea. The flight to Egypt and the return repeat Israel’s story.
The Shema: the Lord our God is the one Lord, and he must be loved with all the heart. Jesus prayed it every morning and every night.
At creation, the Spirit of God was moving over the waters. At the Jordan the Spirit comes over the waters again: a new creation begins.
The dove came back to Noah’s ark with an olive twig, a sign of a new world. At the baptism, the Spirit comes down like a dove.
Israel wandered forty years in the desert and fell in the test. Jesus spends forty days there and overcomes with the very words of Deuteronomy.
Moses went up Mount Sinai and came down with the law. Jesus goes up a mountain and teaches the law of the kingdom with his own authority.
Every fifty years debts were forgiven and slaves were set free. In Nazareth, Jesus announces that God’s great jubilee arrives with him.
God fed his people with manna in the desert. Jesus feeds thousands and says he is the true bread come down from heaven.
The psalm describes God calming the storm and bringing the sailors to harbor. In the boat, Jesus does what only God does.
When God came to save, the blind would see and the lame would leap. Jesus’s miracles show that day has come.
Nathan told David the story of a rich man who stole a poor man’s only little lamb. David got angry and ended up acknowledging his own sin.
God promises that he himself will search for his lost sheep. Jesus, by telling the story of the lost sheep, presents himself as that shepherd.
David went up the Mount of Olives weeping when his son betrayed him. Jesus, the Son of David, goes up the same mount betrayed by a friend.
The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Jesus quoted it that same week in the temple.
God promises a new covenant, written on the heart. At the last supper, Jesus gives the bread and the cup a new meaning.
Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham answers that God will provide it. According to tradition, Jerusalem stands on those mountains.
Centuries before, the psalm describes the mocking, the pierced hands and feet and the clothes gambled for. It ends with a victory: the ends of the earth turn to the Lord.
God will destroy death forever and wipe away the tears from every face. Jesus’s resurrection is the beginning of that.
Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones that come back to life by the Spirit of God. The empty tomb announces that new life.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.
In that culture, an older man didn’t run in public. The father sets aside his dignity and hugs him before anyone can humiliate him.
At the last supper, Jesus starts washing his disciples’ feet, a job for the lowest-ranking servants.
At dawn they haul in 153 large fish, and the net doesn’t tear. On the beach a charcoal fire, fish and bread are waiting for them.
For each temptation, choose the answer from Scripture rightly understood. Careful: the devil also quotes a psalm, but out of context. Then come the same three voices, as they sound today.
A man blind from birth washes in the pool of Siloam and comes back seeing. Jesus says: I am the light of the world.
Don’t just stare at the signpost: go where it points. John wrote these signs so that we believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life (John 20:31).
Behind the rock opens a low cave, blackened by old campfires. The shepherds of Bethlehem kept the lambs here on cold nights. It was common to use caves as stables.
Under the lid there’s a cool cellar with craftsman’s tools: wood and stone, like the trade the Gospel attributes to Jesus in Nazareth.
A cistern carved into the rock to collect rainwater, now dry. In the Bible, Joseph was thrown into an empty cistern, and so was the prophet Jeremiah.
Among the reeds there’s a damp cave where clean water springs up. In the Jordan, Naaman dipped seven times and was healed.
A large cave with niches in the walls. In Elijah’s time, Obadiah hid a hundred prophets in caves and brought them bread and water.
In the mud of the shore the hull of a first-century fishing boat appears. In 1986 one like it was found on the shore of the Sea of Galilee.
A basin carved into the rock for treading grapes, with a channel to a lower vat. Jesus spoke of an owner who planted a vineyard and dug a winepress.
An old well someone had covered. Isaac reopened the wells the Philistines had filled in. Under the lid, a stone staircase goes down to the water.
A narrow tunnel carved into the rock carries the water to the pool of Siloam. King Hezekiah had it dug so the city would have water during a siege.
An abandoned quarry where stone was cut for Jerusalem. Archaeologists believe Golgotha was an old quarry outside the walls.
A first-century tomb carved into the rock, with a round stone that rolls along a groove. That’s how the Gospels describe the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathea.

South of Bethlehem, Herod the Great built a mountain-shaped fortress: the Herodium. In 2007 his tomb was found there. The king who wanted to kill the child ended up buried a few kilometers from where Jesus was born.

By the gate of Bethlehem there’s an old well. Once, hiding in a cave, David longed to drink water from this well. Three of his mighty men crossed through the enemy to bring it to him, and he didn’t drink it: he poured it out as an offering to the Lord.
Under a house there’s a storeroom where the synagogue kept its worn-out scrolls. That’s where the kids of Nazareth learned to read, with the Law of Moses.
A cave by the southern road, the kind travelers used to sleep in. Along a road like this the family fled to Egypt, at night and without delay.
A cave in the hills of the Judean desert, with fire marks and a corner for sleeping. John the Baptist lived in the desert until he began to preach.
Under the rubble appears the mosaic floor of a first-century synagogue. In 2009 a stone carved with a seven-branched lampstand was found in Magdala.
A storeroom under a house in Capernaum. Roofs were made of beams, branches and packed mud: that’s why the paralyzed man’s friends could open one and lower him in front of Jesus.
Among the bushes on the hill there’s a hollow with stacked wicker baskets. After the miracle, the disciples gathered twelve baskets full of pieces.
A staircase goes down to a pool surrounded by columns. In Jerusalem the pool of Bethesda was found, with its five porches, where Jesus healed a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years.
Under the upper room there’s a cool cellar with wine jars and the Passover dishes, ready for the supper.
At the foot of the Mount of Olives there’s a cave where olives were pressed. An ancient tradition says the disciples rested there on the night of the arrest.
A burial chamber with stone boxes for bones. In 1990 an ossuary was found in Jerusalem with the name of Caiaphas, the high priest who judged Jesus.
A dry cave with sealed jars. In 1947, in caves like this by the Dead Sea, the Great Isaiah Scroll was found, copied about a hundred years before Jesus.
When I was a girl, my dad took me to the well before dawn. He said the freshest water is the one you go for early. Later I learned the psalmist spoke of seeking God like that, early in the morning.
My husband was a shepherd. One winter night he went out to look for a single missing sheep and came back at dawn, soaked and happy, with it on his shoulders. I never forgot his face.
I had seven children. Each one went their own way, but on the Sabbath they come back to my table. I always set an extra plate, in case someone comes who has nowhere to go.
They say there’s a teacher in Galilee who sits at the table with tax collectors and fishermen. I’m old now, but I’d like to see him once before I go.
There used to be a leper on the outskirts whom no one went near. I left bread for him on a stone. I never knew his name, but he always waved to me.
I was with the sheep that night, in the fields of Bethlehem. Suddenly a light surrounded us and an angel spoke to us. We were terribly afraid.
We went running and found the baby lying in a manger, just as we had been told. I went back to my flock praising God. I didn’t sleep that night.
Once, coming back from the Passover, his parents searched for him for three days. They found him in the temple, talking with the teachers. Mary never forgot that.
That night we caught nothing. At dawn, the teacher told Peter to let down the nets again, farther out.
We caught so many fish that the nets were breaking and both boats nearly sank. Peter fell to his knees in the boat. Then he left everything and followed him.
I was sick for twelve years. I spent everything on doctors and kept getting worse. I thought: if I touch even his clothes, I’ll be healed.
I came up from behind, through the crowd, and touched the edge of his cloak. At that instant I knew I was healed. He turned around, looked at me and called me daughter.
I used to go for water at noon, when no one was around, so they wouldn’t look at me. That day a Jewish man was sitting by the well, tired from the road.
He asked me for a drink and then told me about a water that takes away thirst forever. He told me everything I had done. I left my jar and ran to town to tell it (John 4).
I was the chief tax collector, and rich. I was short, so I climbed a sycamore tree to see him pass by.
He stopped right underneath, called me by name and said he was going to stay at my house. That day I gave half of what I had to the poor and paid back four times as much to anyone I had overcharged.
I was blind and begged at the entrance to Jericho. When I heard Jesus was passing by, I shouted with all my strength, even though they told me to be quiet.
I was coming in from the countryside and ran into a condemned man. The soldiers forced me to carry his cross behind him.
I walked beside him to Golgotha. I never saw anyone suffer like that without cursing anyone. That cross changed my life.
We were walking sadly back to Emmaus. A man came up to us on the road and explained everything the Scriptures said about the Messiah.
At the table he broke the bread and our eyes were opened: it was him. We ran back to Jerusalem that same night. Our hearts were burning.
When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
